question: Can orchestral movement tell a story without imitating every sound?
intro: Rapid runs and low orchestral gestures make one of the set’s most physical portraits. The initials name an organist, but Elgar’s story concerns his dog rather than his instrument.

sections.label: XI · Dan in the river
sections.mNote: rapid falling figures and vigorous responses

cues.title: Fast lines against a low foundation
cues.text: Quick violin figures fall across a firmer lower line. Listen to the contrast between rapid movement and the weight below it, rather than trying to translate every note into an action.
cues.evidence: Novello pp. 74–81, rehearsal figures 47–51. The opening has rapid violin figures against lower-string motion; no literal sound effect is inferred from the audio.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: George Robertson Sinclair and Dan
cues.text: George Robertson Sinclair is the organist of Hereford Cathedral. Elgar explains that the variation pictures Sinclair’s bulldog Dan falling into the River Wye, paddling ashore and barking—not organs or cathedrals.
cues.evidence: The Elgar Society recounts the incident; the work account reproduces Elgar’s explicit distinction between Sinclair’s profession and the subject of the music. This reports the composer’s story, not independently witnessed events. https://elgar.org/3enigma.htm https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: PDF pp. 74–81, rehearsal figures 47–51. Whole-variation passage map, using the early crest near 0:10, lighter 0:15–0:20 span, and the report’s renewed weight after 0:24. Desk activity is approximate within each window.

timeline.note: Rapid descending string figures begin the portrait (p. 74).
Bassoon motion and stronger wind replies join the string figures (pp. 74–75).
Accented brass and wind gestures add weight to the first surge; percussion punctuates the exchange (pp. 75–76).
The middle exchange lightens to wind figures over continuing string motion (pp. 77–78).
The renewed surge restores brass and percussion weight around the running strings (pp. 78–80).
A final string rush and emphatic orchestral gestures bring the portrait to its short close (pp. 80–81).

composer.epithet: A Worcester violinist who made orchestral variations into portraits of friends and the concerto into an argument with memory.
facts: Largely self-taught; violin, organ, orchestral playing and his father’s Worcester music shop
Bandmaster, Worcester County Asylum, Powick, 1879–84 · organist, St George’s Catholic Church, 1885–89 · Master of the King’s Musick, 1924–34
Two completed symphonies; violin and cello concertos; choral works; chamber music; five completed Pomp and Circumstance marches
composer.background:
Elgar learned the orchestra from inside it. His father William kept a music shop in Worcester, tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church. Edward read the scores in the shop, played violin in local ensembles, taught several instruments and eventually succeeded his father at the organ. He was born in Lower Broadheath in 1857, a Catholic in a predominantly Anglican musical establishment and a tradesman’s son in a profession increasingly organised around London colleges. He remained sensitive to both distinctions throughout his later success. His practical education taught him how a phrase feels under a bow.

At Powick he wrote quadrilles and polkas for an unusual ensemble, learning to give each instrument useful work. The Three Choirs Festival brought larger repertory within reach: Handel, Mendelssohn and contemporary oratorio, alongside orchestral music from the Continent. Visits to London widened that education. Wagner mattered particularly: the chromatic connection between chords, the orchestral recollection of earlier events and the long postponement of a cadence all entered Elgar’s language. His mature scores acquired part of their English character through their subsequent public use.
